headline: Boys in care. Need to be seen too.
intro: Training that helps your team stay alongside boys in care when they push adults away.

problem.scene: 11pm. Dylan, 15, kicks a hole in a door.
problem.question: Within a month: arrested, excluded, moved 40 miles away.
without: A police call for a home matter
with: One team plan around each boy
problem.standards: The 2018 national protocol says the police should be a last resort for incidents a reasonable parent would manage at home.
problem.evidence: The DfE's figures for 2025 show boys make up 56% of children in care in England. Most of what people practise works with girls too, and we say so in the room.

groups: Foster carers and supervising social workers
Pastoral, behaviour and inclusion staff, and designated teachers
Youth justice, early help and youth workers, and personal advisers

outcomes: Describe how one incident becomes a police call, an exclusion and a move, from the boy's side.
Recognise the fear, shame and loss that can sit underneath anger or withdrawal.
Use Bowlby and Siegel's window of tolerance to explain why anger can feel safer than sadness.
Apply the 2018 national protocol to decide when an incident can be managed without the police.
Use PACE and side-by-side conversation to build trust with a boy who avoids talking face to face.
Plan a restorative conversation, and agree a team plan with named actions.

pillars.title: The four restorative questions
pillars.stance_line: Used after an incident so a boy can repair it, rather than be punished and moved.
items: Hear his side first, calmly, once everyone is back in their window.
Help him see who the incident touched, including himself.
Make room for the feeling underneath, not only the behaviour.
What do we do to put it right?
Agree a way to repair it, so he can stay.
pillars.base: Restorative approaches come first under the 2018 national protocol on reducing unnecessary criminalisation.

story_line: Dylan, 15, and Josh, 12, run through the day. Both are composites, drawn from real experiences of care.

facilitator.name: Luke Rodgers BEM
facilitator.line: From care leaver to care leader
paras: Luke went into care at 10. He has spent his career inside children's services as a consultant, trainer and keynote speaker, and is CEO of The Care Leaders.

He has worked with councils and the NHS nationally on children whose behaviour leads to moves, including Durham's children's homes, where he put NVR into 11 homes, and Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent, where more than 400 staff were trained.
He led the national engagement on England's new fostering standards for the Department for Education, so he knows what the standards expect of the adults around a child.
He was a Knowledge Equity Fellow at Saïd Business School, University of Oxford, and was awarded the British Empire Medal in 2018 for commitment to children and families.
